sections.html: Salminus brasiliensis (formerly S. maxillosus) is a characin rarity that grows to up to 1 m and over 20 kg. It is a migratory species.

The dorado, Salminus brasiliensis, is a large characid from Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, Uruguay and Argentina, growing to 100 cm SL. A highly prized game fish in some of its native waters, it turns up as juveniles in some aquatic stores, but it is not suited to captive life in any respect. Housing one for life is beyond the reach of virtually all hobbyists.

  • Needs a tank at least 2 m long
Primarily a riverine species, but is also found in lakes and ponds.

A truly humongous tank (or pond) would be required by an adult specimen, as it's an incredibly fast-swimming, active, predatory fish. Something in the region of 6 m x 1.2 m x 1.2 m should be considered a bare minimum. A tank like this would hold over 9000 litres of water!
Even young animals should have large aquariums available.

Speaking hypothetically, decor would not be critical. Obviously, an enormous filtration system would be needed to cope with the massive amounts of biological waste a fish like this produces. A decent amount of flow through the tank would also be needed.
Highly piscivorous in nature, juvenile captive specimens have been known to accept prawns, lancefish etc. An adult fish would need large amounts of fish such as whole trout. An expensive proposition!
As strong devourers, their appetite cannot be satisfied with flake food in the long term. Sometimes a defrosted fish should be fed.

Will not eat anything it can't fit into its mouth, but this doesn't leave many available species with which it could be housed in the long term. Young fish have been seen cohabiting with large tankmates such as Cichla sp., arowana and other tankbusting fish.

Migrations take place from October to January and are correlated with the rise of the water levels as well as the rising length of day. The fish follow their prey on their migrations to the spawning grounds. In both migratory behaviour and appearance Salminus species recall salmon, and like them they are threatened by dams, barrages and environmental pollution.

In aquaria their rowdiness must be considered: with their strong teeth they can hurt their tankmates.
Impossible in home aquaria. Should not even be considered an option.
As an esteemed food fish, it is farmed in Brazil.

The common name of this species is derived from the Portuguese dourado and refers to the beautiful golden colour of the fish. It is included purely because an alarming number of juvenile fish have been showing up in some aquatic stores and, as a result, in hobbyists' tanks. This species is simply not suited to captive life in any respect. If you see one for sale, and they are undeniably an attractive fish, please don't be tempted to buy it. As responsible fishkeepers we should consider the long term well-being of any fish that we buy, and housing a dorado for life is beyond the reach of virtually all hobbyists. Sadly, owning this species and others like it seems to be fashionable at the moment, with some aquarists even viewing them as a status symbol. It is to be hoped this situation can be rectified in the future, as surely all these aquarium specimens are doomed to a premature death. It's a highly prized game fish in some of its native waters.
